newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM remains party's leader despite criticism.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM remains party's leader despite criticism.

text.p: The ruling Czech Civic Democratic Party (ODS) on Sunday re-elected Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus as its chairman despite signs of discontent within the party over his forceful leadership and mixed election results.
Klaus ran unopposed at the party's national congress in the second city of Brno.
"It is a great responsibility and I know that it will require a lot of work, and a lot of vigour," the Czech CTK news agency quoted Klaus as saying to the delegates after the vote.
Klaus, who has been chairman of the party since it was founded in 1991, won 249 out of the 295 ballots cast.

But party leaders at the congress continued to stress that lingering questions must be addressed if ODS is to remain at the forefront of Czech politics, where it has been since winning general elections in 1992.
Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec, who was re-elected as one of four party vice-chairmen, repeated his recent warnings that a gulf was growing between ODS and the country's electorate.
"They are problems to which we should grant attention in the future," the agency quoted Zieleniec as saying. "Let's consider ways to show a more friendly face to citizens."
But he insisted to party delegates on Saturday that the problems lay "more in style than in content".
The governing three-party coalition lost its majority in mid-year elections to the lower house of parliament.

Czech voters then snubbed Senate elections in November, with a roughly 30 percent turnout. Those who voted gave ODS 32 of the new upper house's 81 seats, despite forecasts that it could win an outright majority.

Chairman Klaus rejected speculation that the party lacked plurality and that internal discussion was stifled under his chairmanship, but added that election results this year had fallen short of party expectations.
The prime minister blamed disappointing electoral results in part on mistakes "at all levels" within the party and called for measures to bring more members into the fold.

Interior Minister and ODS member Jan Ruml, who declined nomination to be a vice-chairman at the congress, said it was important that Klaus signalled an awareness that "within ODS everything is not all right and we're simply at a crossroads where we ought to decide how to proceed."
Just months ago, the vigorously self-confident right-wing economist Klaus seemed invincible after four years of internationally acclaimed free-market reforms.
But persistent appeals for more voices to be heard within ODS have been seized upon by opposition leaders and others anxious to expose cracks in the dominant party's armour.
